title: In the Monty Hall puzzle, switching doors doubles your chance to win
body: You pick one of three doors: one hides a car, two hide goats. The host, who knows where the car is, always opens a different door to show a goat, then offers you a switch. Your first pick was right only 1 time in 3, and the host’s reveal doesn’t change that, so the 2 in 3 chance that the car was elsewhere now rests entirely on the one remaining door. Switching wins two-thirds of the time.

slides.alt: Animation on a game-show stage: you pick door 1 and the host opens door 3 to show a goat. Then 300 simulated games fill two bars, switching winning 202 and staying 98, and a diagram shows the 2 in 3 chance of the other two doors moving onto door 2.
slides.music: “Happy Happy Game Show” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.heading: Play it out
slides.text: Say the car is behind door 1. Pick door 1 and switch: you lose. Pick door 2 or 3: the host must reveal the other goat, so switching wins. Two wins out of three.

slides.heading: Switching wins the car in 2 games out of 3
slides.note: Sticking with your first door wins only when that first 1-in-3 guess was right.

slides.heading: Imagine 100 doors
slides.text: You pick one, and the host opens 98 doors with goats, leaving one closed. Sticking with your 1-in-100 first guess suddenly looks far less tempting.

slides.question: When columnist Marilyn vos Savant said switching wins, some 10,000 readers wrote in. Out of 10, how many held a PhD?
slides.explanation: About 1 in 10: close to 1,000 of the letters came from PhD holders, many on the letterhead of maths and science departments, and most of the letters insisted she was wrong. She was right.

slides.heading: Experts got it wrong
slides.text: When Marilyn vos Savant explained the answer in 1990, about 10,000 readers wrote in, nearly 1,000 of them PhDs, mostly insisting she was wrong.

slides.heading: The rules matter
slides.text: It all hinges on the host knowingly avoiding the car. If he opened a door at random and it just happened to show a goat, switching would only be 50/50.

slides.question: What changes if the host opens a door at random and it just happens to show a goat?
slides.explanation: The 2-in-3 edge depends on the host knowingly avoiding the car. If his reveal was pure luck, switching is only 50/50.
